OSHA is a Weather-Ready Nation Ambassador committed to working with NOAA and other Ambassadors to strengthen national preparedness for and resilience against extreme weather.
Introduction
An earthquake is a sudden, rapid shaking of the ground caused by the breaking and shifting of rock beneath the Earth's surface. This shaking can damage buildings and bridges, disrupt utilities, and trigger hazards such as landslides, avalanches, flash floods, fires, and tsunamis. Structures built on unstable soil are especially vulnerable. Buildings, trailers, and manufactured homes not anchored to reinforced foundations can also be shaken off supports. All 50 states, five U.S. territories and the District of Columbia face some level of earthquake risk, which can occur at any time of the year.
When an earthquake strikes a populated area, it can cause deaths, injuries, and widespread property damage. However, ground shaking itself is rarely the direct cause of most injuries and deaths. Instead, people are typically hurt by collapsing walls or floors, flying glass or objects, or by trying to move during the shaking.
Footage from the 1964
Great Alaska Earthquake
illustrates the scale of destruction earthquakes can cause. During this event, liquefaction triggered a major landslide in the Turnagain Heights area. Liquefaction takes place when loosely packed, water-logged sediments at or near the ground surface lose their strength in response to strong ground shaking. Liquefaction occurring beneath buildings and other structures can cause major damage during earthquakes.
Areas most vulnerable to liquefaction include coastal zones, riverbanks, beaches, and floodplains with loose, water-saturated soils such as sand and silt, often where shallow water tables and artificial fill exist. In the United States, high-risk regions include the San Francisco Bay area and the Los Angeles Basin.
These webpages provide information on earthquake hazards, preparedness, and the precautions workers and employers should take after an earthquake.
The
Preparedness
page outlines how employers and workers can get ready for an earthquake by creating an emergency response plan, providing workplace training, sharing essential information, and assembling emergency supply kits.
The
Response/Recovery
page explains the key hazards to avoid after an earthquake, such as dangerous driving conditions, unstable structures, falling objects and debris, and offers guidance to help protect worker safety and health.
